scope_findings.claim: The project builds one harmonised multisensory observation chain that integrates omics, in-situ, airborne and satellite data for ecosystem condition assessment and predictive modelling.
Three omics layers enter the chain: metabolomic measurement, genomic and transcriptomic sequencing, and environmental DNA metabarcoding.
The observation chain runs from in-situ plots through field spectroscopy and uncrewed aerial survey to Copernicus satellite data.
Three demonstration cases cover terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems along one agricultural pressure gradient from farmland through freshwater ecotones to coastal waters.
Cases target habitats and ecotones the topic marks as under pressure or as restoration priorities, selected on evidence rather than data availability.
The pressures driving each case are analysed as socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems.
A knowledge-gap and data-need analysis runs before the integration design and prioritises critical biodiversity knowledge gaps.
Deep-learning models scale habitat classification and ecosystem mapping from the three cases to European coverage and predict biodiversity trends, using AI-assisted mapping.
Predictive modelling of biodiversity trends is delivered at case, regional and European scales.
The project delivers FAIR data, harmonisation workflows and processing protocols supporting data integration from genome to space.
The multi-season field archive is reworked into documented training and validation datasets with a declared split protocol, and its use is verified on the demonstration cases.
Every habitat label the project publishes carries a crosswalk to the Global Ecosystem Typology and EUNIS.
Harmonisation workflows and data are published with provenance and linked to the European Open Science Cloud and the European Common Data Spaces.
Commission-steered grassland and agricultural-landscape monitoring data (LUCAS grassland, EMBAL) is ingested as a reference layer for the terrestrial case.
Effort and budget are earmarked for cooperation with the named in-situ data collection frameworks GBIF, OBIS and LUCAS, and project occurrence records are published to them.
The project provides a standing coordination interface to the space-agency earth-observation projects of the ESA FuturEO programme.
The interoperability work package holds an open, zero-funding place for the Joint Research Centre, counted towards no eligibility condition.
Outputs are shaped to reporting obligations under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framework Directive and EU Nature Restoration Regulation.
The project contributes its harmonisation decisions to standards bodies, supporting joint definitions of data collection, metadata and processing protocols.
Where a European research infrastructure offers a service the chain needs, the project uses it rather than rebuilding it.

Biodiversity indicators derived from the chain are carried into farm-management decision-support tools through a multi-country user network of agricultural holdings, and practitioners are evaluated on whether they can act on them.
scope_findings.flag_reason: Borderline against loaded Tier 2B scope. SR-04 requires linking observation data to agriculture (and other sector) data and to data infrastructures; it does not name carrying biodiversity indicators into farm-management decision-support tools as a required scope element. The concept traces this uptake activity to the call extract's scope_summary phrase ('biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture'), which is not present in scope_requirements.json or call_constraints.json. Confirming this claim in_scope would rely on a scope element outside the loaded Tier 2B authority; scope boundary is defined by Tier 2B only. Nearest element is SR-04, pending confirmation against a Tier 2B scope element.
